This Week in Democracy: A Fund Falls, an Attorney General Rises, and Citizenship Is Tested Again

Force-feedings, birthright citizenship orders, and a journalist's prosecution mark a week of institutional strain

```markdown This week in Washington was shaped by one long argument over who controls the machinery of law enforcement, and by a series of smaller ones over who controls the border, the courts, and the truth. By week's end, the fight over the attorney general's office had been resolved in the president's favor, even as several others remained open.

The week began over the weekend with Trump pressuring the Senate to confirm Todd Blanche, his former personal attorney, as attorney general, while threatening to simply leave Blanche in the acting role indefinitely if senators would not yield. At issue was a $1.8 billion fund that critics said was designed to compensate Trump's political allies and potentially shield his family from tax audits — an arrangement Republican holdouts wanted addressed before they would vote to confirm. Elsewhere over the weekend, Trump Media rolled out a premium Truth Social subscription tier selling early access to market-moving presidential posts for up to $100,000 a month, even as the administration sought $10 million in taxpayer money to cover event costs. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History came under executive pressure over alleged political bias, and Arizona's supreme court ruled that clergy who learn of child abuse through confession have no duty to report it — a decision arising from a case in which three children continued to suffer abuse for years after bishops privately learned of it. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. urged parents to vaccinate against measles while simultaneously repeating misinformation about vaccines, a contradiction unfolding against a 35-year high in measles cases. Ethics concerns also touched Congress: the House ethics committee recommended censuring Rep. Chuck Edwards for staff harassment, while Senator Bernie Moreno called publicly for Rep. Max Miller's resignation over abuse allegations raised by his own daughter.

By Monday, litigation became the week's dominant register. A coalition of 25 states — eventually joined by others, including two Republican governors — sued in the Court of International Trade to challenge tariffs imposed on goods from 60 trading partners, arguing the measures exceeded the president's statutory and constitutional authority. That same day, court records and detainee video surfaced showing that ICE had sought court orders to force-feed hunger strikers in at least ten cases, alongside documentation of contaminated drinking water at a California detention facility, often affecting detainees without legal counsel. In North Carolina, the state Senate passed a voter-restriction bill without debating Democratic amendments, removing protesters from the gallery in the process, while the House scheduled votes on companion legislation restructuring courts and elections along more partisan lines. Trump also turned his public anger on U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro after the Justice Department dropped vandalism charges related to a Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool incident that Trump had earlier mischaracterized online — a dispute that would resurface later in the week. Meanwhile, at the state and local level, Washington's governor signed legislation restricting license plate readers, and Monroe County ended its surveillance camera contract early, following reporting that documented 28 cases of officers misusing plate-reader data to track people in their personal lives. At an international terrorism conference, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and adviser Stephen Miller made unsubstantiated claims characterizing left-wing violence as widespread and warranting elimination "by any means necessary."

Tuesday was comparatively quieter but not without consequence. ICE detained a Johns Hopkins pharmacy researcher and a University of Maryland pharmacy instructor at separate airports despite both holding valid work authorization; each was eventually released. A federal judge issued a split ruling on New York's ICE transparency law, blocking the requirement that agents show their faces and identification during enforcement actions while allowing the state's separate ban on local police cooperation with ICE to remain in place. Reporting also revealed that federal contractors building the Arizona border wall were broadly exempted from environmental laws, including protections for an endangered bird species. The allegations against Rep. Miller deepened as Senator Moreno detailed specific claims of physical abuse, adding pressure ahead of a looming candidate-replacement deadline. And a dark-money nonprofit called One Nation began a $1.7 million disinformation campaign against Senator Ossoff, generating 78 million impressions with claims that contradicted his actual voting record — a story that would expand considerably by week's end.

Wednesday brought a notable moment of direct democracy alongside further executive and press-related conflict. Missouri voters rejected a measure to eliminate the state income tax by an overwhelming 83.3 percent, along with a related phaseout amendment defeated by similar margins, while renewing a conservation sales tax — a rare instance of voters decisively rebuffing tax-cut ideology despite being outspent by the measure's proponents. New Mexico's attorney general sued the Department of Justice, alleging it had stonewalled the state's criminal investigation into Jeffrey Epstein's activities at Zorro Ranch by missing a deadline to hand over unredacted records. Trump's legal team, meanwhile, moved to block a court-ordered financial disclosure to the BBC ahead of a deadline while pressing forward with a separate $10 billion defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal. The Justice Department also issued, then quietly withdrew, subpoenas to New York Times reporters covering Air Force One security matters. In immigration enforcement, ICE deported a man to Guatemala one day after a federal judge had ordered his removal halted, later calling it a case of mistaken identity; his lawyer said he would be returned. Separately, a former immigration judge sued over what she described as a politically and demographically motivated termination, and federal employees filed a class action challenging the elimination of gender-affirming care coverage.

Thursday marked the week's most direct constitutional confrontation. Trump signed two executive orders narrowing birthright citizenship and targeting birth tourism — just over a month after the Supreme Court had ruled 6-3 that his original 2025 order attempting the same thing was unconstitutional. The same day, the Justice Department petitioned the Supreme Court to lift a block on mail-ballot restrictions while continuing its 30-state lawsuit demanding voter registration data, a suit that had by then been rejected by 21 different judges. The Department of Homeland Security separately demanded that four states purge their voter rolls, threatening prosecution of officials who declined. A Senate subcommittee obtained a backup of Dr. Anthony Fauci's government-era iPhone and voted to refer him for contempt after he had invoked Fifth Amendment protections in an earlier hearing. Journalist Georgia Fort was charged with conspiracy for documenting an anti-ICE church protest — charges that later unraveled somewhat when the Justice Department conceded that false information had been submitted to judges in at least 15 warrant applications and to a grand jury in her case. A senior DOJ official reportedly urged prosecutors to "go big" against immigration protesters, a directive tied to at least one Texas case resulting in decades-long sentences. ICE and TSA rapidly expanded airport enforcement targeting people with pending visa and asylum applications, prompting some airlines, including Southwest, to begin resisting agents who lacked judicial warrants. Trump also threatened lengthy prison sentences for officials who leaked reports of U.S. munitions shortages during the Iran conflict, while twenty-four states sued to block a federal demand for welfare recipients' immigration data, and the Senate passed a Russia sanctions bill granting the president broad new tariff authority.

The week closed on Friday with the resolution of its central storyline: Senator Bill Cassidy, the last Republican holdout, announced his support for Blanche, clearing the way for confirmation after weeks of negotiation over the anti-weaponization fund, which had ultimately been rescinded as the price of his ascension. On the same day, Trump signed two more executive orders further narrowing birthright citizenship, calling the Supreme Court's ruling "very unfortunate" and describing his new orders as mere "adjustments" — language that left little ambiguity about the administration's view of judicial finality. New figures showed ICE had detained more than 43,000 people in July, the highest monthly total of the term, while further reporting detailed the prolonged force-feeding of at least ten hunger strikers over months, an FBI decision not to investigate a fatal ICE shooting, and the termination of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and South Sudanese despite ongoing crises in both countries. A new body-camera policy was also revealed to allow ICE to withhold footage of killings from the public. Still, the week's record was not one-sided: an analysis found federal judges had ruled against the administration in 75 of 93 First Amendment cases — a rejection rate far higher than under the prior administration — even as Fort's attorneys moved to have her indictment dismissed on First Amendment grounds. The One Nation disinformation campaign against Ossoff was revealed to be part of a broader network of fake local news sites targeting six states with competitive Senate races, funded through undisclosed dark money and paid social promotion. The Justice Department's own internal watchdog, meanwhile, was found to have been gutted, its staff cut from 29 to 16 and its director fired with no replacement, even as misconduct complaints reached their highest level since 2005. The week ended with smaller but familiar notes of conflict of interest: a sitting federal appeals judge had run a private firm for months after confirmation, and senators were reported to be delaying a hemp product ban at the administration's request, in a move benefiting a company tied to the White House chief of staff's son-in-law.

Taken as a whole, the week traced a familiar but sharpening pattern: an executive branch testing the outer edges of judicial rulings it found inconvenient, an enforcement apparatus expanding with fewer visible checks, and a press and judiciary that, however unevenly, continued to push back. The confirmation of a president's former personal lawyer as the nation's chief law enforcement officer, arriving alongside new executive orders that treated a Supreme Court ruling as negotiable, will likely be remembered less as an isolated news cycle than as a marker of how far institutional boundaries were tested — and, in the Missouri vote and the courts' First Amendment record, where they still held. ```
